revise

/rih-VYZE/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Revise means to reconsider and make changes to something, especially a written work, in order to improve it.

After reading the judges' comments, Tomás stayed up late to revise his competition essay, cutting the weak opening and adding stronger evidence.

Example

The playwright spent the whole summer working to revise her second act: she reconsidered every scene, cut a character who slowed the story, and rewrote the ending twice before the script finally felt right.

She didn't just reread the act — she reconsidered it and made changes to improve it. That combination of looking again and changing for the better is the heart of revise.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rework: Rework means to shape the material again from a fresh angle — a scene rebuilt around a different character, an essay reorganized around a new thesis. Revise is wider and calmer: reconsider the work and change whatever needs improving, large or small. All reworking is revising; much revising is gentler than reworking.

amend: Amend means to alter something formally, usually to correct or improve it — laws, contracts, and official records are amended. Revise belongs to drafts and working texts: a writer reconsiders and changes their own pages to make them better. Parliaments amend a bill; writers revise a chapter.

polish: Polish means to refine the small details until the writing shines — smoothing sentences, sharpening word choices, perfecting what already works. Revise can cut far deeper: reconsidering structure, arguments, and whole passages. Polishing is the finishing touch at the end; revising can rebuild the middle of the work.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

preserve: to keep exactly as written, without changes

neglect: to leave something untouched and unimproved

Where it sits · how much of the work is changed

tweak → revise → overhaul

tweak vs. revise: To tweak a draft is to make one or two tiny adjustments — far lighter than to revise it, which means rethinking the whole piece to improve it.

overhaul vs. revise: To overhaul a draft goes further than to revise it: you tear it down and rebuild it from the ground up.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: again, back (Latin)

Root — vis-: to see, to look at (Latin videre/visere)

Put it together: "revise" literally means "to look at again" — you return to your own work, see it with fresh eyes, and change what those fresh eyes reveal.

Use the root in a new word: supervise: The head baker stayed late to supervise the new apprentices in the kitchen.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral, school and publishing

Revise is the standard word for improving a draft, and its related noun form is revision — both the act of revising and the changed draft itself. One caution: in British English, revise can also mean to study for an exam; the SAT tests the 'rework a text to improve it' sense.
